questions.question: At a bakery with one server, which of the following situations is an example of a customer balking?
options: A customer is turned away because the shop has room for only $K$ customers and is full.
A customer arrives, sees six people waiting, and decides not to join the queue.
A customer is refused entry by the shop because the predicted wait exceeds 10 minutes.
A customer joins the queue, waits 15 minutes, and then leaves before service.

questions.question: In an M/M/1/K queue with Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, arrivals are blocked only when the system is full. Which entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)$, for $n$ jobs present, describes this blocking?
options: $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ for all $n\ge0$
$\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda(K-n)/K$ for $n\le K$ only
$\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda\,\mathbf{1}\{n<K\}$ for all $n\ge0$
$\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda$ for all $n\ge0$

questions.question: Consider a single-server queue with balking, entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ when $n$ jobs are present and service rate $\mu$. Why is this queue stable for every choice of $\lambda>0$ and $\mu>0$, even when $K\lambda>\mu$?
options: Because the mean entry rate $\lambda^{+}$ always equals the potential arrival rate $K\lambda$.
Because balking customers are served later, so no work is lost from the system.
Because stability only needs $\lambda<\mu$, which the balking factor guarantees.
Because nobody enters at $n\ge K$, so the number in the system never exceeds $K$.

questions.question: For a single-server queue with balking, entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ when $n$ jobs are present and service rate $\mu$, potential customers arrive at rate $K\lambda$. Which rate should be used in Little's law $\mathbb{E}[L]=(\text{rate})\cdot\mathbb{E}[J]$ to obtain the mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$ of an entering customer?
options: The mean entry rate $\lambda^{+}=\sum_{n}\lambda^{+}(n)p(n)$
The potential arrival rate $K\lambda$ of all customers
The service rate $\mu$ of the single server
The parameter $\lambda$ of the entry-rate formula

questions.question: In a queue with balking, customers arrive at rate $\lambda(n)$ when $n$ jobs are present, and the level-crossing equation reads $\lambda^{+}(n)p(n)=\mu(n+1)p(n+1)$. What does $\lambda^{+}(n)$ count?
options: All customers who arrive while $n$ jobs are present, whether or not they join
Only the customers who arrive while $n$ jobs are present and actually join
The customers who arrive while $n$ jobs are present and decide to balk
The customers who complete service while $n+1$ jobs are present

questions.question: In a single-server queue with balking, the entry rate is $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ with $K=5$ and $\lambda=2$ per hour. At what rate do customers enter while $n=3$ jobs are present?
options: $6$ per hour
$0.4$ per hour
$4$ per hour
$10$ per hour

questions.question: Potential customers arrive at a single server, and a customer who finds $n<K$ jobs present joins with probability $(K-n)/K$, where $K=6$. What is the probability that a customer who finds $n=2$ jobs present balks?

A single-server queue with balking has entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$, with $K=3$, $\lambda=1$ and $\mu=2$ per hour. Using the level-crossing recursion $p(n+1)=\lambda^{+}(n)p(n)/\mu$, what is $p(1)/p(0)$?

A single-server queue with balking has entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ with $K=2$ and $\lambda=1$ per hour. The time-average probabilities are $p(0)=8/13$, $p(1)=4/13$ and $p(2)=1/13$. What is the mean entry rate $\lambda^{+}$ of customers who join?
options: $24/13$ per hour
$20/13$ per hour
$12/13$ per hour
$2$ per hour

questions.question: A single-server queue with balking has service rate $\mu=4$ per hour, and the server is idle a fraction $p(0)=0.25$ of the time. What is the mean entry rate $\lambda^{+}$ of customers who join?
options: $1$ per hour
$0.75$ per hour
$3$ per hour
$16$ per hour

questions.question: For a single-server queue with balking, entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ when $n$ jobs are present and service rate $\mu$, the fraction of potential customers who balk is computed as $\sum_{n=0}^{K}p(n)\,n/K$, with $p(n)$ the time-average probabilities. Which assumption justifies weighting with $p(n)$?
options: The service times are exponential with rate $\mu$.
The queue is stable, so $p(n)$ exists for every $n$.
Each customer balks with probability $n/K$ independently.
Potential customers arrive as a Poisson process.

questions.question: Compare a single-server queue with balking, entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ when $n$ jobs are present and service rate $\mu$ with a single-server finite calling population of $N=K$ sources, each generating a request at rate $\lambda$ while not in the system. Which statement about their time-average probabilities $p(n)$ is correct?
options: They are equal, because both have birth rates $\lambda(K-n)$ and death rate $\mu$.
They are equal only when $\lambda=\mu$, since only then the rates coincide.
They differ, because the calling population has a state-independent arrival rate.
They are equal only if the calling population has $N=K+1$ sources.

questions.question: For a single-server queue with balking, entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ when $n$ jobs are present, $K\ge2$ and service rate $\mu$, potential customers form a Poisson process with rate $K\lambda$. Why is the mean entry rate $\lambda^{+}=\mu(1-p(0))$ rather than $K\lambda(1-p(K))$?
options: Because $p(K)=0$ in the balking model, so the second formula would give $K\lambda$.
Because customers also balk below level $K$, while departures occur at rate $\mu$ whenever $n\ge1$.
Because $\mu(1-p(0))$ and $K\lambda(1-p(K))$ are always equal in a stable single-server queue.
Because the service rate is smaller than $K\lambda$, so the server limits the throughput.

questions.question: A single-server queue with balking has entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ with $K=3$ and $\lambda=\mu=1$ per hour. Which vector is proportional to $(p(0),p(1),p(2),p(3))$?

Potential customers arrive as a Poisson process at rate $4$ per hour at a single server; a customer finding $n<2$ jobs joins with probability $(2-n)/2$. The time-average probabilities are $p(0)=0.2$, $p(1)=0.4$, $p(2)=0.4$. What fraction of potential customers balks?

Potential customers arrive as a Poisson process at rate $2$ per hour at one server with $\mu=2$ per hour and capacity $K=2$. Under balking a customer finding $n$ jobs joins with probability $(2-n)/2$; under blocking everyone joins while $n<2$. What fractions of potential customers are lost?
options: balking $2/5$, blocking $1/3$
balking $1/5$, blocking $1/3$
balking $1/3$, blocking $2/5$
balking $2/5$, blocking $1/7$

questions.question: For a single-server queue with balking, entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ when $n$ jobs are present and service rate $\mu$, keep $K\ge1$ and $\mu$ fixed and let $\lambda\to\infty$. Which describes the limiting behaviour of the mean entry rate $\lambda^{+}$ and the balking fraction $1-\lambda^{+}/(K\lambda)$?
options: $\lambda^{+}\to0$, since the system is almost always full; the balking fraction $\to1$.
$\lambda^{+}\to\mu$ and the balking fraction $\to1$.
$\lambda^{+}\to\infty$ and the queue becomes unstable; the balking fraction $\to1$.
$\lambda^{+}\to K\mu$ and the balking fraction tends to $1-\mu/\lambda$.

questions.question: For a single-server queue with balking, entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[K-n]^{+}$ when $n$ jobs are present and service rate $\mu$ and $\lambda>0$, nobody enters at level $K$, since $\lambda^{+}(K)=0$. Which statement about the top level $K$ is correct?
options: $p(K)=0$, because no customer enters while $K$ jobs are present.
$p(K)/p(K-1)=K\lambda/\mu$, because the potential arrival rate is $K\lambda$.
$p(K)>0$ and $p(K)/p(K-1)=\lambda/\mu$, since $\lambda^{+}(K-1)=\lambda$.
$p(K)>0$, but the system can also reach level $K+1$ at rate $\lambda$.

questions.question: At a single server with balking, $\lambda^{+}(n)=\lambda[3-n]^{+}$ with $\lambda=1$ and $\mu=3$ per hour, so potential customers arrive at rate $3$ per hour. The stationary probabilities are $p=(9,9,6,2)/26$ for $n=0,1,2,3$. What is the mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$ of an entering customer?
options: about $20.8$ minutes
about $62.3$ minutes
about $22.5$ minutes
about $31.8$ minutes

questions.question: Potential customers arrive as a Poisson process at rate $6$ per hour at a single server with service rate $\mu=4$ per hour. A customer who finds $n<3$ jobs present joins with probability $(3-n)/3$, and nobody joins when $3$ jobs are present. What fraction of the potential customers balks?
